column1: What gap in Module 1's `@Input()` knowledge does Module 2 close?
column2: Module 1 only showed reading an `@Input()` once, safely, in `ngOnInit`. Module 2 covers what happens when an `@Input()` value CHANGES after the component already exists — `ngOnInit` never runs again, so a different mechanism is needed.

column1: In an Angular component hierarchy, can a grandchild component pass data directly to its grandparent, or a component talk directly to a sibling?
column2: No. Data only flows down via `@Input()` to a DIRECT child, and events only flow up via `@Output()` to a DIRECT parent. There is no built-in shortcut — communication across levels or between siblings must be relayed one hop at a time through the parent (or later, via shared services with DI).

column1: Why is 'the parent is the switchboard' the standard pattern for sibling communication?
column2: Angular provides no sibling-to-sibling binding mechanism — templates only bind to their own direct children. Routing all shared state through one parent also keeps data flow traceable: you can inspect one component to understand the whole feature's state.

column1: If a grandchild component needs to affect a distant ancestor, how must the event travel?
column2: It must be relayed one level at a time: the grandchild emits `@Output()` to its direct parent, whose handler explicitly re-emits its own `@Output()` (or calls a method) that its own parent listens to, and so on up the tree.

column1: Why doesn't `ngOnInit` re-run when a parent updates an already-set `@Input()`?
column2: `ngOnInit` is a strictly one-time hook — it fires only once, right after the FIRST input assignment. It has no mechanism to detect or react to subsequent changes.

column1: What are the two ways to react to a changing `@Input()`, and when should you use each?
column2: An `@Input()` setter (`@Input() set prop(value) {...}`) for reacting to ONE input with simple logic. `ngOnChanges` for reacting to MULTIPLE inputs together, or when you need the PREVIOUS value for comparison.

column1: What information does an `@Input()` setter give you that a plain `@Input()` property does not?
column2: It lets you run code every time the parent assigns a new value to that specific input — a plain property only gets read passively wherever you access it, with no hook into the moment it changes.

column1: Why must you replace an `@Input()` object/array instead of mutating it in place (e.g. `this.settings.maxLength = 200`)?
column2: Angular's default change detection and `ngOnChanges` compare objects BY REFERENCE. Mutating properties in place keeps the same reference, so Angular may not notice the change. Replacing it (`this.settings = {...this.settings, maxLength: 200}`) gives a new reference Angular can detect.

column1: Why should you always type `EventEmitter<T>` with a specific type instead of leaving it untyped?
column2: An untyped `EventEmitter()` defaults to `EventEmitter<any>`, which compiles but silently loses the type-safety net that would otherwise catch a parent handler expecting the wrong data shape.

column1: When should a child component NOT use `@Output()` to expose a value?
column2: When the value is only for live display and the parent already owns the source data — the parent can often compute what it needs directly, without a round-trip through the child. `@Output()` is for cases where the child knows something the parent doesn't (like exact keystroke timing).

column1: Which three lifecycle hooks are in Module 2's scope, and what does each represent?
column2: `ngOnChanges` (fires on every @Input() change, including the first), `ngOnInit` (fires exactly once, after the first ngOnChanges), and `ngOnDestroy` (fires exactly once, right before the component is removed).

column1: What is the guaranteed order of: constructor, `ngOnInit`, and the first `ngOnChanges`?
column2: constructor → ngOnChanges (first call) → ngOnInit. ngOnChanges fires before the first ngOnInit, once inputs are set.

column1: Why is `implements OnChanges, OnInit, OnDestroy` worth adding even though Angular calls these methods by name regardless?
column2: It's a free TypeScript correctness check: without the interface, misspelling a hook name (e.g. `ngOnDestory`) silently means the method never runs, with no warning. With the interface implemented, TypeScript catches the typo at compile time.

column1: What does the `SimpleChanges` object passed to `ngOnChanges` contain?
column2: It's keyed by input property name; only inputs that actually changed that cycle appear. Each entry has `currentValue` (the new value), `previousValue` (the value before this change), and `firstChange` (true only on the very first call).

column1: If a component has two `@Input()`s and only one changes, what does `ngOnChanges`'s `changes` parameter contain?
column2: Only a key for the input that actually changed — the unchanged input does not appear in the `SimpleChanges` object at all, which is why you must guard with `if (changes['propName'])` rather than assuming.

column1: Inside `ngOnChanges`, if you read `this.text` directly, do you get the old or new value — and how do you get the old value?
column2: `this.text` already holds the NEW value by the time `ngOnChanges` runs (the class property is already updated). To get the old value, use `changes['text'].previousValue` — the only place the previous value is still available.

column1: Why does `ngOnChanges` exist when `ngOnInit` already handles the first `@Input()` assignment?
column2: `ngOnInit` never runs a second time, so it can't react to data that changes AFTER creation. `ngOnChanges` runs on every subsequent change, which is exactly what a live-updating display (like character counts) needs.

column1: Give the core distinction between `ngOnInit` and `ngOnChanges` in one line each.
column2: `ngOnInit`: fires exactly once, after the first `ngOnChanges` — for one-time setup. `ngOnChanges`: fires every time a bound `@Input()` changes, including the first — for reacting to data that keeps changing.

column1: In the Character Counter's 'Clear text' scenario, why would putting the count-recalculation logic in `ngOnInit` alone be a real bug?
column2: The counts would compute once on creation and then FREEZE — never updating again no matter how many times the parent's text changes or is cleared, since `ngOnInit` never re-runs.

column1: Does `ngOnChanges` fire on a component that has zero `@Input()` properties?
column2: No — with nothing bound to compare, there's nothing to report. Use `ngOnInit` (or the constructor, for non-Angular setup) instead for components without inputs.

column1: What is `ngOnDestroy`, and when does it fire?
column2: A lifecycle hook that fires exactly once, immediately before Angular removes a component from the DOM entirely — whether from `*ngIf` becoming false, an `*ngFor` item being removed, or navigation away.

column1: Why does Angular need `ngOnDestroy` — what kinds of things don't clean themselves up automatically?
column2: A running `setInterval`/`setTimeout`, a native `addEventListener` listener, or an ongoing subscription all keep running/firing even after the component's markup disappears, unless explicitly cancelled — leaving them uncleaned causes a memory leak.

column1: What is a 'memory leak' in the context of Angular components?
column2: A resource (timer, listener, subscription) that outlives the component that created it because it was never cleaned up in `ngOnDestroy` — the browser keeps a reference alive pointing at a component instance that should have been garbage-collected.

column1: In the TypingIndicatorComponent example, what does `ngOnDestroy` do and why?
column2: It calls `clearTimeout(this.idleTimeoutId)` to cancel any pending timer before the component is removed, preventing a leaked callback from trying to update a property on a component instance that no longer exists.

column1: By default, when a change-detection pass runs, what does Angular do across the component tree?
column2: It walks EVERY component in the tree top to bottom, re-evaluates every template expression against current property values, updates only the DOM pieces that differ, and calls `ngOnChanges` for any child whose `@Input()` bindings changed during the walk.

column1: What role does Zone.js play in Angular's change detection?
column2: It patches async browser APIs (DOM events, setTimeout/setInterval, Promises/fetch) so that whenever one of these fires, Angular is notified and runs a change-detection pass across the whole component tree.

column1: How can a single keystroke in `TextInputComponent` cause `StatsPanelComponent` (a sibling) to update, with no direct connection between them?
column2: The keystroke triggers one whole-tree change-detection pass: the `@Output()` updates the parent's `text` property, which flows down as a new `@Input()` to `StatsPanelComponent`, triggering its `ngOnChanges` — all within that same pass.

column1: Is `ngOnChanges` the same thing as 'change detection'?
column2: No — change detection is the much bigger tree-walk-and-compare mechanism that runs automatically; `ngOnChanges` is just one small consequence of that process, specifically for `@Input()` changes.

column1: Do you need to manually trigger a re-render after a normal `(click)`/`(input)` handler updates a property?
column2: No — change detection already runs automatically after any Zone.js-patched event. Just update the property; Angular re-checks all bindings on its own right after the handler returns.

column1: What later-module optimization does the 'always replace, never mutate' `@Input()` habit from this module set you up for?
column2: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush` — an opt-in strategy that skips checking a component unless its `@Input()` references actually changed (or an event originated inside it), which only works correctly if inputs are always replaced rather than mutated.
